# Evaluation Results

Full-corpus run: **47 documents** (Docling parser, 4,215 chunks), golden set of
**25 Q&A**. Generated by `accurag evaluate data/golden/golden.jsonl --answer-quality`.

## Complete comparison (retrieval + answer quality)

| Config | Faithfulness | Answer Rel. | Recall@5 | MRR | P95 Latency (ms) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| dense (naive) | 0.988 | 0.776 | 0.867 | 0.803 | 670 |
| hybrid (dense+sparse, RRF) | 0.978 | 0.776 | **0.947** | 0.828 | 454 |
| hybrid + rerank (Cohere) | 0.984 | **0.808** | 0.933 | **0.861** | 1208 |

**What the numbers say (honestly):**
- **Faithfulness ~0.98 across the board** — the grounded prompt (answer only from the
  numbered context, else "I don't know") genuinely prevents hallucination; answers
  stay tied to the retrieved context that is returned verbatim as the sources.
- **Answer relevancy ~0.78** — moderate, dragged down by honest "I don't know"
  refusals on questions the corpus doesn't fully cover (a refusal scores ~0 on
  relevancy by design). Reranking's better context nudges it up to 0.808.
- **Hybrid wins recall@5 (0.947)** by adding lexical/sparse matching; **rerank wins
  MRR (0.861)** by floating the right chunk to rank 1 — but its recall@5 (0.933)
  dips just under hybrid because it truncates the over-fetched set. Rerank trades a
  little recall for better top-rank precision. Not a clean sweep — a real tradeoff.

## Methodology

- **Answer quality is judged by a custom lightweight LLM judge, not Ragas.** Ragas
  pulls the langchain ecosystem and broke on a missing `langchain_community`
  vertexai import; a small OpenAI-SDK judge (`accurag.evaluate.judge_answer_quality`)
  is leaner, transparent, and avoids that dependency hell. **Judge ≠ generator:** the
  judge is `gpt-4o-mini`; answers are generated by Claude. Faithfulness and answer
  relevancy are scored 0–1 per question and averaged.
- **Context Precision/Recall (the LLM-judged retrieval columns) are still `—`** —
  we report the deterministic retrieval metrics (recall@5, MRR) instead; the judged
  context columns are a future add.

## Doc-level vs chunk-level labels (precision tightening)

The portable `golden.jsonl` labels relevance at **document** level. A stricter set,
`golden_chunks.jsonl`, labels the **exact answer-bearing chunks** — built by
`scripts/build_golden_chunk_labels.py` via TREC-style pooling (union of dense+hybrid
candidates per question, each judged for relevance by gpt-4o-mini). 23/25 questions
got chunk-level labels (avg ~4.9 relevant chunks each); 2 fell back to doc-level
(e.g. the "why this project *excludes* GraphRAG" meta-question — not in any paper).

| Labels | dense Recall@5 | dense MRR | hybrid Recall@5 | hybrid MRR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| doc-level | 0.867 | 0.803 | 0.947 | 0.828 |
| chunk-level | 0.518 | 0.743 | 0.527 | 0.723 |

**Reading it honestly:**
- Recall@5 falls ~0.95 → ~0.53 **not because retrieval degraded** but because (a) it
  now requires the *specific* chunks, and (b) there are ~4.9 relevant chunks/question
  vs only k=5 slots, so recall@5 is mathematically capped low (|relevant| > k).
- **MRR holds (~0.72–0.74):** the rank-1 result is still usually a truly relevant
  chunk — the metric that stays interpretable at chunk granularity.
- At chunk level **dense ≈ hybrid** — hybrid's doc-level recall lead was partly just
  "retrieved *some* chunk from the right doc." Tighter labels exposed that.
- Chunk-level labels are **index-specific** (they reference Docling's chunk ids), so
  `golden.jsonl` (doc-level) stays the portable set for the cross-parser A/B.

## Chunk-size sweep (pymupdf token-window path)

Which chunk size searches best? Ingested the corpus at 256 / 512 / 800 tokens
(pymupdf parser) and scored each on the doc-level golden set
(`scripts/chunk_size_sweep.py`).

| chunk_size | #chunks | dense Recall@5 | dense MRR | hybrid Recall@5 | hybrid MRR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 256 | 4,201 | 0.880 | 0.781 | 0.920 | 0.840 |
| **512** | 1,721 | **0.893** | **0.838** | **0.933** | 0.890 |
| 800 | 1,045 | 0.853 | 0.810 | 0.933 | **0.893** |

**512 tokens wins** (best/tied-best on 3 of 4 metrics) — a textbook curve, now
measured for this corpus:
- **256 (too small):** worst ranking (dense MRR 0.781) — chunks lack enough
  context for the right one to rise to the top.
- **800 (too big):** worst dense recall (0.853) — coarse chunks blur the match;
  hybrid's lexical matching rescues it.
- **512:** strongest dense metrics, tied-best hybrid. This **validates the
  `chunk_size=512` default** with evidence rather than a guess.

(Hybrid recall is flat across sizes — sparse/lexical matching makes retrieval
robust to chunk size; the dense metrics are where size shows.)

## A measured non-result: rerank candidate depth

A paper *in this corpus* — *From BM25 to Corrective RAG* — ablates reranker depth
and reports that feeding the cross-encoder only 20 candidates is ineffective
(its Recall@5 0.458). `hybrid_rerank` over-fetched exactly 20, so the obvious move
was to deepen the pool. Measured on our golden set:

| hybrid_rerank | Recall@5 | MRR |
|---|---|---|
| 20 candidates | 0.933 | 0.861 |
| 50 candidates | 0.893 | 0.853 |

**Deeper was slightly worse, not better** — so it wasn't adopted (default stays 20,
tunable via `rerank_candidates`).

The *why* is measurable. Hybrid first-stage recall by depth (doc-level):

| depth | 5 | 10 | 20 | 50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| recall | 0.947 | 0.947 | 0.947 | 0.947 |

**Flat.** Every relevant document the first stage will ever find is already in the
top 5; nothing sits at ranks 6–50 to recover. The paper's "20 is too shallow"
premise needs recall still *climbing* past 20 (true on harder text-and-table
retrieval); ours is saturated. So a deeper pool hands the reranker only extra
distractors — pure downside. The lesson isn't the 0.04 — it's that a grounded,
plausible improvement was *measured* and rejected (with a mechanism), not shipped
on faith. Deeper reranking pays off only where first-stage recall is still rising
at that depth.

## Vision figure extraction (`ingest --vision`) — works, with a sharp caveat

The only retrieval failures on this corpus are figure/chart-heavy docs whose data
lives in images (doc 41 = 4 charts, 0 tables). `ingest --vision` renders each
figure and has a vision model (gpt-4o-mini) describe it into a searchable text
chunk (`{doc}-figN`). Measured on doc 41:

- **Before:** figure-data questions → *"I don't know"* (the data isn't in any text
  chunk). Confirmed.
- **After:** for a figure-targeted query, the figure chunks rank **#1–3**, and
  `ask()` returns a **grounded, cited** answer from `41-fig0`. A previously
  unanswerable question becomes answerable.

**The caveat (important).** gpt-4o-mini reads chart *structure* reliably (titles,
axes, series, datasets, metric cutoffs) but **guesses bar/line heights** — the
extracted numeric values are noisy. So a *quantitative* chart answer comes back
**grounded but numerically wrong** ("9.9, 4.9, 2.9, …" — meaningless). And
deterministic source attribution **does not catch this**: it guarantees the
source chunk is real and was the one used, not that the chunk read the number
correctly off the chart. Vision opens a new failure mode — confidently-wrong
quantitative answers that are faithful to a mis-extracted source.

**Verdict.** Keep `--vision` as an opt-in for figure-heavy corpora: reliable for
*"what does this figure show / what's compared / at what cutoffs"* (structure),
**not** for *"what's the exact value"* — on the cheap model. The first non-retrieval
change that moved the needle — honestly bounded.

### Model escalation: gpt-4o-mini vs Claude Sonnet (measured)

Same doc-41 chart (% Failed Retrievals @ 20), both models:
- **gpt-4o-mini misread the structure** — it collapsed a 5-panel (per-dataset) ×
  6-embedding-model grid into a flat per-dataset list. Wrong layout → meaningless
  numbers.
- **Claude Sonnet parsed it correctly** — 5 dataset panels, the 6 models on each
  axis (Voyage-2, Voyage Large-2, Cohere Multilingual/English v3.0, Gemini 001/004),
  6 method series, as a clean Model × Method table with pattern-consistent values.

**Verifiable signal:** Anthropic's contextual-retrieval eval did use Voyage, Cohere,
and Gemini embeddings — Sonnet *recovered those real model names off the axes*;
gpt-4o-mini missed them. So Sonnet demonstrably read the chart and gpt-4o-mini did
not — the gap is "wrong vs right structure," not marginal.

**Two-tier recommendation.** gpt-4o-mini for bulk/simple figures (cheap); **route
dense / multi-panel / quantitative charts to Claude Sonnet.** The cheap model is
fine until a chart actually carries data in its bars.

(Note: the measurement injected doc 41's 4 figure chunks into the live
`accurag_docling` index by hand; a clean build is `accurag ingest --parser docling
--vision`.)

## Honest caveats (read these)

1. **Latency is indicative, not benchmarked.** P95 includes the OpenAI query-embed
   call (~0.5 s) and, for rerank, a Cohere **Trial key** (10 calls/min) whose
   backoff can inflate the number under load. Treat dense/hybrid (~0.5 s) as
   representative; rerank as an upper bound.
2. **Golden labels are doc-level.** `relevant_chunk_ids` hold manifest doc ids, so
   recall@5 / MRR are computed at document granularity (a retrieved chunk `12-3`
   counts for relevant doc `12`). Chunk-level labels would tighten this.
3. **Index built with the Docling parser** (structure-aware `HybridChunker`). See the
   parser A/B below for how this compares to the fast PyMuPDF lane.

## Sample grounded answers (hybrid + rerank)

- *"How does reciprocal rank fusion combine multiple ranked lists?"* → correct,
  with the exact RRF formula and `k=60`, **sources `12-0`/`12-1`** (the RRF
  paper) returned with the answer.
- *"What is contextual retrieval and how does it improve RAG?"* → **"I don't know"**
  — and on investigation this is **correct behavior**, not a bug.
  The corpus contains only the *Contextual Retrieval **Appendix*** (doc 41 — a
  table of benchmark recall numbers), not the prose blog post that explains the
  technique. So no answerable definition was ever ingested, and the grounding
  guard rightly refused instead of hallucinating. (Earlier draft wrongly blamed
  the chunker; the real cause is corpus coverage.) Note doc 41 *is* table-dense
  and PyMuPDF flattened its tables to linear text — so a **table-value** query on
  doc 41 is exactly where a structured parser (Docling) should beat PyMuPDF, and
  is a good target for the parser A/B.

## Parser A/B: PyMuPDF vs Docling (same golden set, same embedder)

Two indexes were built from the same 47 docs — one with `--parser pymupdf`
(fast, token-window chunks) and one with `--parser docling` (memory-safe config:
pypdfium2 backend + TableFormer FAST; structure-aware `HybridChunker`). Docling
peaked at **~4.3 GB across the whole corpus** (single process) and produced
**4,215 chunks vs PyMuPDF's 1,772**.

| Index | dense Recall@5 | dense MRR | hybrid Recall@5 | hybrid MRR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| pymupdf | 0.853 | 0.787 | 0.933 | 0.817 |
| **docling** | **0.867** | **0.803** | **0.947** | **0.828** |

**Docling wins, but marginally** on aggregate retrieval. The sharper signal is the
**table-value question on doc 41** (the Contextual-Retrieval benchmark appendix):
- pymupdf ranked doc 41 at **position 3** (behind unrelated doc-38 chunks);
- docling ranked doc 41 at **position 1** — structured chunking surfaced the
  table-dense doc first;
- **both still answered "I don't know"** — the question requires comparing
  multiple table rows, and neither retrieved context carried the full comparison,
  so the grounding guard correctly refused in both.

**Conclusion:** structured parsing gives a small-but-consistent retrieval lift and
clearly better ranking of table-heavy docs. Docling costs ~2.4× the chunks (≈2.4×
embedding) and ~14 min vs ~2 min to ingest. So: **Docling is the quality default
where tables matter; PyMuPDF is the fast/cheap lane** — selectable via `--parser`,
and now backed by numbers.

### Root cause of the doc-41 "I don't know" (investigated, hypothesis disproved)

I initially blamed **table→text serialization** for the doc-41 failure. The data
disproved it: parsing doc 41 with Docling reports **4 figures, 0 tables, 67 text
blocks**. The contextual-retrieval failure-rate numbers are rendered as **bar
charts (images)**, not text tables — so there is *nothing to serialize better*. No
text parser (Docling or PyMuPDF) recovers numbers from chart images with OCR/vision
off (our deliberate no-GPU constraint). The only extracted text is the chart's
intro sentence and axis labels ("1 minus recall @ 20").

**So the real levers for this class of question are NOT parsing serialization:**
1. **Vision / chart extraction** (a VLM or OCR+chart-understanding pass) — out of
   scope here (no GPU); a "what I'd do next" item.
2. **Corpus curation** — ingest the *prose* Contextual-Retrieval blog post, not just
   its chart appendix, so the explanation is actually present.

This is the eval-first method working: a plausible hypothesis (serialization),
measured and rejected, pointing at the true cause (image content + corpus coverage).

## Reproduce

```bash
accurag ingest --parser pymupdf            # ~2 min, all 47 docs
accurag evaluate data/golden/golden.jsonl  # the table above
accurag ask "How does reciprocal rank fusion work?" --strategy hybrid_rerank
```
